THE CAR CHOKED ACTIVITY CENTRE OF COBURG. The picture says it all. The activity centre is nearly 50% car park and we have no plans to change it. Two generations of poor planning and over accommodating the motor vehicle is why we have a transport problem. We need to reshape Moreland with a more balanced plan. 
Reduce car spaces by 25% across all of our local destinations and watch how short car trips start to get replaced with walking and cycling. 
To give you an example, there are three people who live within 100 metres of my house who use their car for a 100-metre-long journey and these are regular trips. There are three others within 100 metres of my house who use their cars for regular 400 metre trips. There are tens of thousands of these trips every day in Moreland. When you oversupply a city with parking, every trip regardless of its distance becomes convenient with a car. Over time our driving habits become culture and eventually you get into a mess like the one we are in now. 
By reducing parking spaces, the short trips are the first to become inconvenient with the car and people eventually switch their short trips to walking and cycling. There is very little difference in the time it takes to make say a 200-metre journey by foot or by car. The car is quicker but by the time you hop in, buckle up, get out of a drive way or possibly do a U-turn and then travel 200 metres, maybe give way along the way, unbuckle when you arrive and get out of your car, it’s going to take you a similar amount of time to walk. If the driver has to also circle around for 2 or 3 minutes looking for a park or be forced to park 50 or 100 metres form the destination, then that short trip is no longer convenient with a car and next time that person will consider walking. Over time our transport culture around short trips changes, we get a better balance and with no one inconvenienced. 
A reduction of car spaces at our local destinations has to be part of our overall transport plan if we are going to create a better balance in the way we travel.

I call on the Member for Frankston Paul Edbrooke MP and Education Minister James Merlino to immediately intervene with the decision to change the Frankston High School Zone. To change the zone during the Victorian Covid 19 crisis when members of the community have lost their jobs, struggle to pay mortgages, falling property prices along with, the largest economic contraction in well over two decades, this decision should be put on hold leaving the current zone intact. The current zone should remain until this crisis has past and the economy has stabilised. Post COVID-19 and economic stabilisation, any review of the zone should include wide community consultation.

The zone change is interesting as the development community will have a financial windfall from the proposed changes with the inclusion in the new zone of the areas between Dandenong Road East and Frankston Freeway freeway as well as, the area along Beach St, resulting in developers advertising developments being in the Frankston High School Zone which will substantial increase  sale prices . I am not against developers receiving good prices for their properties; however, this should not be at the expense of current property owners in the current zone.
A fairer approach for any changes to the zone should be an expansion of the current zone to include the new areas.  This would mean current property owners and families would not be disadvantaged (especially during these difficult times) and those in the new areas could take advantage of any increased property price as a result of the zone expansion. Paul Edbrooke MP and James Merlino please display some leadership to right this wrong.

We need to make sure that Glen Eira remains clean and green for generations to come. We need to take action now!

Not only is a healthy natural environment beautiful, it also provides major positive health benefits for all of our residents. Council has a major role to play in tackling the climate emergency, supporting communal efforts in moving towards renewable energy, and endorsing appropriate environmental standards for developers. It’s not an easy task, but we can work smarter, not just harder, using forward thinking, evidence-based and innovative solutions to protect and preserve our natural environment. 

To start, our Council’s Urban Forestry Strategy simply isn't good enough. Currently, the strategy aims to increase tree cover by 1.5% by 2040, a number significantly lower than all surrounding Councils. I know we can do better. Improved tree cover lowers temperatures, improves air quality, and supports active transport such as walking and cycling. As your next councillor, I will fight strongly to overhaul our Urban Forestry Strategy so that it’s more ambitious and actually makes an impact.

I think there’s also room to work in how we support local businesses and residents wishing to transition to renewable energy. From financial support grants to programs like the Solar Saver Scheme, there are so many ways we can improve support for more green development. Not only will I advocate for greater investment in things like solar panels on council and community property, but I’ll also look at improving the standards set around the environment for developments in general. Not only will it save us money in the long-term through lowering electricity costs, but it will go a long way in helping us fight against climate change.

As your next councillor, I will also fight diligently to ensure that our Council upholds its commitment to Carbon Neutrality. The climate emergency is exactly that. An emergency. All levels of government will need to play their part, and I know that in Glen Eira, we can do so much better.

That’s why i will:
① Expand Council support to businesses and residents transition to renewable energy
② Develop a more ambitious Urban Forestry Strategy
③ Ensure Council upholds its commitment to Carbon Neutrality
④ Ensure new developments are held to the highest environmental standards

Open Letter | Community 

Our region is a great place to live and raise a family and, frankly, I love the Rockhampton region. We have talented and creative people, a diverse economy with great opportunities and a sense of pride in our community. We come together and help people in need and we roll-up our sleeves in the face of natural disasters and for important causes.

I believe Council needs to be at the forefront of community development and making our region a better place for everyone − no matter what job you have, where you live or what school you go to. As a volunteer and active member of the community, I’m always committed to helping people in need and making sure no one gets left behind. 

I believe Council has an important role in bringing everyone together, genuinely engaging people in decision-making and making our community kinder and more welcoming for all.

Last Friday I released my Community Development Policy, setting out my vision for more community engagement, greater partnerships with community groups and a commitment to increase inclusion across the Rockhampton region.

I’m particularly interested in delivering a Rockhampton Community Development Strategy, a blueprint for making our region a better place to live and to help foster a more inclusive community.

Down at Livingstone, new Mayor Andy Ireland has put in place Consultative Committees for each Portfolio area. I’m hearing positive reports about these forums strengthening consultation and leading to real input into Council decision-making. 

If elected, I’d like to launch the same in Rockhampton: seven Portfolio Roundtables would comprise community members and be about providing Councilors and Executives with feedback and insight into initiatives and Council’s strategic agenda.

I also want to work with stakeholders to build the case for a Neighborhood Centre. Let’s find a site and develop a strategy to build a purpose-built modern facility for use by community groups and not-for-profit organisations. A Neighbourhood Centre is badly needed in Rocky; I know it would help strengthen our community. I know this would require funding from other levels of government, but I know how vital these centres are in other towns across Queensland.

We have an amazing community in the Rockhampton region, but we do have some challenges. Whether it's homelessness and rental affordability, childhood disadvantage, drug and alcohol abuse, domestic violence or unemployment, I believe we’re best placed to tackle these and other challenges as a united community, working together to get the best outcomes for the Rockhampton region. 

I want to lead a community that is inclusive, supportive and working together to build a bright future for the Rockhampton region.

Nyree Johnson

Written and authorised by N Johnson, 61 Lucas Street, Berserker QLD 4701

If you’re worried about overdevelopment in Labrador, Biggera Waters and Chirn Park please sign this petition to Parliament👇👇👇
https://www.parliament.qld.gov.au/work-of-assembly/petitions/petition-details?id=3493

It’s been started by Jenna. She runs the Labrador 4215 Facebook group/page.

It’s actually the first petition I’ve been asked to sponsor as an MP and I think it sensibly lays out the very real concern of overdevelopment.

Jenna has done so much to foster the community in our area and to keep people informed. She knows how fearful many residents are about the proposed changes to the City Plan. 

One of the major issues she’s raised is that the scale of the changes to Labrador and Biggera Waters should have meant there was a higher level of consultation by the Council. 

Things like ads in the Bulletin and opening up ‘unprecedented’ rounds of formal consultation often don’t engage people and are just there to tick a box. 

Instead of ‘informing’ residents of the changes and asking for their feedback, they should have involved residents more from the beginning of the process. 

Remember when all this came out in late 2019 and it was a complete shock for so many people? 

Another issue raised is the Council has chosen suburbs which don’t have all the requirements for this growth. They also weren’t named in the State Government’s SEQ Regional Plan. 

This is the plan that details how many people the Government expects our region to grow by, leaving it up to the Council to figure out how to manage that growth locally.

If successful, the petition will hopefully mean the State Government will need to look into what engagement the Council has undertaken to see whether it’s been enough.

Hello all. I’ve decided to run again in the Moreland City Council election in October. I will be running for one of three positions in the South Ward. 
It’s been a challenging few months for my family and I, yet we have been more fortunate than many. My heart goes out to all those who have lost family and friends to this devastating virus.
I spent the last three months thinking whether this was a good time for campaigning about other issues. Eventually I felt that addressing the sustainability of our way of life is more important than ever. 
This is the third major virus in 18 years. While it is too early to tell whether this is a result of humankind and our impact on nature, the three major things I am campaigning for will not only help us now, but will also contribute to a healthier and more sustainable future. 
 
ACTIVE TRANSPORT
If there is ever a time to get people walking and cycling, it’s now. Even before Covid19, the United Nations recommended that governments spend 20% of their total transport budget on active transport. The Andrew’s government spends less than half of 1%. Our state and federal governments have no interest in active transport and we can’t wait around for that to change. 
It’s up to us. 
Walking and Cycling would represent a larger share of our total trips and most of our local trips if we had the infrastructure in place. 
A network of separated and off-road bike lanes connecting our schools, shops, parks, tram stops and train stations must be one of Moreland’s top priorities over the next 10 years. 
The Moreland Integrated Transport Strategy, (MITS), including its 10-year cycling plan, is a good start but we need to do more to fill in the gaps and have a chance to meet the targets that we have set for modal share and carbon emissions.

TREES ARE EVERYTHING!
They cool our homes, provide shelter for walking, give cover from rain, increase land values, attract birds, reduce noise pollution, conserve water, minimise soil erosion, save energy, supply food and absorb carbon dioxide. They shouldn’t be removed for profit or pruned by the lowest bidder. They should be treated like our greatest asset not like a financial bargaining chip. 
It’s not just about planting 5000 trees a year, which is a great effort, it’s also about taking care of existing trees and allowing them to create an urban forest environment like no other.

SUSTAINABLE PLANNING
There are many ways we can reshape our city into a more sustainable one, with better quality developments, more open space and a safer and better balance in the way we travel. Some of these include
• Land contributions from developers instead of cash contributions with the purpose of creating new open space and active transport corridors.
• Rejecting high density housing that isn’t close enough to public transport.
• Rewarding our sustainable residents with lower taxes.
• Expanding the Park Close to Home plan so we can work towards interconnecting our open space with a new walking and cycling network.
• Expanding the Sustainable Design Standards program to support developers anyway we can to encourage more sustainable developments.

I hope you will have time to read my flyers and Facebook posts over the next couple of months and get a feel for how we can take advantage of the potential Moreland has in becoming a more productive, healthy and sustainable city.

Authorised by George Georgiou, 9 Mathieson St, Coburg North.
